questions.q: A security model outputs a number between 0.0 and 1.0 representing how likely a network connection is to be an attack (e.g. 0.87). Is this classification or regression, and how should it be evaluated?

choices.A: Classification, because the number is used to make a security decision
choices.B: Regression, because the output is a continuous number -- and it should be evaluated with accuracy/F1 exactly like classification
choices.C: Regression, because the output is a continuous number -- so it should be evaluated with MSE/RMSE-style metrics, not accuracy/F1
choices.D: Neither -- probability scores don't fit into either category

questions.explanation: The card's own example lists a 0.0-1.0 risk/probability score as a regression output (continuous number), which means regression metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE) apply -- not classification metrics like accuracy or F1.

questions.q: You train a malware classifier on 10,000 files, then test its accuracy on those SAME 10,000 files. It scores 99.9%. Should you trust that number?

choices.A: Yes, 99.9% is 99.9% no matter how you measured it
choices.B: No -- testing on training data mostly measures memorization, not how the model performs on new, unseen malware
choices.C: No, because malware classifiers can never legitimately exceed 50% accuracy
choices.D: Yes, as long as the original split ratio was 80/20

questions.explanation: This is the train/test split concept: evaluating on data the model already memorized just proves it can recall answers, not that it generalizes. That's why you always hold out a separate test set it never saw during training.

ctf_question.q: SCENARIO: You're pentesting a company's phishing-email detector -- a supervised classifier trained on labeled phishing vs. legitimate emails. You have no access to its code, but testing shows it leans heavily on suspicious keywords and link count as signals. You start rewriting your phishing emails' wording and restructuring their links -- keeping the same malicious payload -- until the model stops flagging them as phishing. What's this technique called?
ctf_question.explanation: This is Feature Manipulation from the 'How Attackers Evade Supervised Models' section -- once you know (or infer) which features a model relies on, you can reshape your input to shift those features across the decision boundary without changing what the input actually does.
